definition: A function with learned parameters: input goes in, a prediction comes out. On disk it is a file of numbers (the weights) plus the code that runs them.
why_it_matters: When a video says "the model", it means this: a big file of numbers and the program that applies them.

definition: Umbrella term for any technique that lets computers do things that normally need human intelligence, from hand-written rules to learned neural networks.
why_it_matters: The whole field. Everything else in this guide is a sub-topic of it.

definition: Sub-field of AI where the program learns patterns from examples instead of being explicitly programmed with rules.
why_it_matters: Solves problems where nobody can write the rules by hand: recognising a face, judging spam, predicting churn.

definition: ML using neural networks with many layers. The approach behind modern vision, speech and language models.
why_it_matters: More layers let the network learn more abstract patterns (edges → shapes → objects; letters → words → meaning). This is what made today's AI possible.

definition: A model built from layers of simple units (neurons) that pass weighted signals forward. Training adjusts the weights.
why_it_matters: The basic machine every deep-learning model, including every LLM, is built from.

definition: Training adjusts the weights using data: expensive, done rarely, by whoever builds the model. Inference runs the frozen weights to get an answer: cheap, done billions of times, by everyone.
why_it_matters: The most important split on the map: stages 3–5 train, stages 6–7 only infer. Prompting and RAG never change the weights.

definition: Models that produce new content (text, images, audio, code) rather than only predicting a label or a number.
why_it_matters: The shift from AI that classifies things to AI that makes things.

definition: A very large neural network (almost always a Transformer) trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. The engine behind chatbots and coding assistants.
why_it_matters: The thing you talk to in ChatGPT or Claude. The central object of this guide; stages 1–7 of Map 2 describe its life.

definition: A big general-purpose model trained once on broad data and then adapted to many tasks. LLMs are the best-known example.
why_it_matters: Train once, expensively; reuse everywhere, cheaply. This economics is why a few labs train and everyone else adapts.

definition: The most capable models available at a given moment, and the handful of companies that train them (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI, and a few Chinese labs).
why_it_matters: "Frontier" in a video simply means "the best there is right now".

definition: A model that handles more than one data type (text + images + audio + video) as input and/or output.
why_it_matters: Lets one model read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, and answer in text. See section 14.

definition: The field of making computers understand and generate human language. LLMs are its current state of the art.
why_it_matters: The older name for the discipline; many pre-2020 techniques (word2vec, BERT, parsing) come from here.

definition: The field of understanding images and video. Historically CNNs, increasingly Transformers (ViT).
why_it_matters: Where deep learning first proved itself (ImageNet, 2012), and where many terms like "convolution" come from.

definition: A discriminative model learns to separate or label inputs (spam / not spam). A generative model learns the distribution of the data, so it can produce new samples.
why_it_matters: Tells you whether a model judges inputs or produces outputs. A spam filter is discriminative; an LLM is generative.

definition: Narrow AI does one task well. AGI would match humans across most intellectual tasks; it is a goal and a debate, not a product.
why_it_matters: When people argue about AGI timelines, this is the term; nothing you can download today is AGI.

definition: The older, rule- and logic-based approach to AI. Contrasts with learning from data. Still used inside planners and some hybrid systems.
why_it_matters: Explains why "AI" in a 1990s product meant if/else rules, and why "neuro-symbolic" means mixing the two.

definition: Learning from examples that come with the correct answer (labels); the model learns input → label. Used in classic ML, in SFT and in reward-model training.
why_it_matters: Most accurate way to learn when you can afford labelled examples. Its limit is the cost of labelling.

definition: Finding structure in data with no labels: grouping, compressing, spotting anomalies.
why_it_matters: Works on data nobody has labelled, which is most data. Finds groups and outliers you did not know to look for.

definition: Supervised-style training where the label is carved out of the data itself, e.g. hide the next word and predict it. This is how LLMs are pre-trained.
why_it_matters: Turns the whole internet into free training labels. The single trick that made LLMs possible at scale.

definition: Mixing a small labelled set with a lot of unlabelled data.
why_it_matters: Gets most of the accuracy of supervised learning with a fraction of the labelling cost.

definition: An agent takes actions in an environment and learns from rewards instead of labelled answers. Used in games, robotics and LLM post-training (RLHF, GRPO).
why_it_matters: Lets a model get better than its teachers: it can discover strategies no example showed it, as long as you can score the result.

definition: The agent is the learner, the environment is what it acts on, the policy is its decision rule (for LLMs: the model itself), the reward is the feedback signal.
why_it_matters: Decode any RL video: "policy" = the model being trained, "reward" = the score it is chasing.

definition: The RL dilemma: try new actions to discover better ones (explore) or repeat what already works (exploit).
why_it_matters: Explains why RL training samples several answers per prompt instead of only the best one.

definition: Classic value-based RL: learn a table (or network) estimating how good each action is in each state. DQN was the 2013 breakthrough that played Atari games from pixels.
why_it_matters: The RL you see in game-playing demos. LLM post-training uses policy-based methods (PPO, GRPO) instead.

definition: Search that looks ahead by simulating many possible futures and focusing on promising ones. Combined with neural networks (AlphaGo) it beat Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016.
why_it_matters: An ancestor of "thinking longer" in reasoning models: spend more compute at decision time to get better decisions. (Today's reasoning models do it with long chains of thought, not tree search.)

definition: Learning a policy by copying demonstrations from an expert.
why_it_matters: SFT is imitation learning: the model copies the ideal answers humans wrote. RL is what lets it go beyond them.

definition: Reusing what a model learned on one task or dataset as the starting point for another. Fine-tuning a pre-trained model is transfer learning.
why_it_matters: Why you never start from zero: a model that already knows language learns your task from a few hundred examples.

definition: Training that pulls representations of matching pairs together and pushes non-matching pairs apart (an image and its caption; two views of the same photo).
why_it_matters: How embedding models and CLIP learn that "a photo of a cat" and the cat picture belong together.

definition: Predicting a category (spam / not spam, cat / dog).
why_it_matters: The most common ML task in business. Next-token prediction is also a classification over the vocabulary.

definition: Predicting a continuous number (price, temperature, time to failure).
why_it_matters: The other basic task; when the answer is a number, it is regression.

definition: Grouping similar items together without labels (k-means).
why_it_matters: Finds natural groups: customer segments, topics in documents, duplicate records.

definition: Compressing many features into fewer while keeping the important structure (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP).
why_it_matters: How people draw 2-D pictures of embeddings: hundreds of dimensions squashed down so you can see clusters.

definition: Flagging data points that do not look like the rest.
why_it_matters: Fraud, intrusion and fault detection: learn what normal looks like, alert on the rest.

definition: The known correct answer attached to a training example.
why_it_matters: The expensive ingredient of supervised learning; its quality caps the model's quality.

definition: Fit a straight line (or hyperplane) to predict a number.
why_it_matters: The simplest model there is; everything else is a more flexible version of "fit a curve to the data".

definition: A linear model for classification that outputs a probability.
why_it_matters: Fast, explainable baseline. If a neural network cannot beat it, something is wrong.

definition: A flowchart of if/else splits on features. Easy to read, prone to overfitting.
why_it_matters: Humans can read the rules it learned, which makes it popular where decisions must be explained.

definition: Many decision trees trained on random subsets of data and features, then averaged.
why_it_matters: Averaging many imperfect trees cancels their individual mistakes: more accurate and far more robust than one tree.

definition: Build trees one after another, each correcting the errors of the previous ones.
why_it_matters: The most accurate choice for tabular data in most competitions and companies. Try this before a neural network.

definition: Finds the boundary with the widest margin between classes.
why_it_matters: A strong pre-2012 classifier; a wide margin makes it generalise well on small datasets.

definition: Predict by looking at the k most similar training examples.
why_it_matters: No training at all, just lookup. The same idea powers vector search in RAG: find the nearest embeddings.

definition: Fast probabilistic classifier that assumes features are independent.
why_it_matters: The classic spam filter; works surprisingly well on text with almost no compute.

definition: Clustering by assigning points to the nearest of k centroids and repeating until stable.
why_it_matters: The default way to split data into k groups when you have no labels.

definition: Linear dimensionality reduction along the directions of largest variance.
why_it_matters: Compresses data while keeping what varies most; used to shrink embeddings and to visualise them.

definition: A feature is one input variable. Feature engineering is hand-crafting better inputs.
why_it_matters: In classic ML, good features matter more than the algorithm. Deep learning's big win is learning features automatically.

definition: Data is divided so you train on one part, tune settings on a second and measure final performance on a third the model never saw.
why_it_matters: The only honest way to know how a model will do on new data. Skipping it is how projects fool themselves.

definition: Rotate which slice is held out and average, for a more reliable estimate.
why_it_matters: Gives a trustworthy accuracy number from a small dataset.

definition: Memorising the training data (great on train, poor on new data) versus being too simple to capture the pattern at all.
why_it_matters: Overfitting is the number-one way models fail in production: perfect in the lab, useless on real inputs.

definition: Simple models err systematically (bias); complex models err erratically depending on the data they saw (variance).
why_it_matters: Explains why bigger is not always better: a model can be too flexible for the amount of data you have.

definition: Penalising large weights to reduce overfitting. L1 also pushes weights to exactly zero.
why_it_matters: Makes a model generalise better by stopping it from relying too hard on any one input.

definition: Stop training when validation loss stops improving, even if training loss is still falling.
why_it_matters: The cheapest protection against overfitting: just stop at the right moment.

definition: A setting you choose before training (learning rate, tree depth, LoRA rank), as opposed to parameters learned from data.
why_it_matters: What engineers tune by hand; a wrong learning rate can make an otherwise good model fail completely.

definition: Combining several models' predictions.
why_it_matters: Usually beats any single model; the same idea as asking several experts and taking the majority view.

definition: A table of predicted class versus actual class, showing where a classifier confuses things.
why_it_matters: Shows which mistakes the model makes, not just how many. Essential when some errors cost more than others.

definition: Precision: of what the model flagged, how much was right. Recall: of what should be flagged, how much it caught. F1 balances the two; ROC / AUC summarises the trade-off across thresholds.
why_it_matters: Accuracy alone lies when classes are unbalanced (99% "not fraud" is 99% accurate and useless). These metrics tell the truth.

definition: Information from the test set, or from the future, accidentally reaching the training data.
why_it_matters: The classic reason a model scores brilliantly in testing and fails in production.

definition: When one class is far rarer than the other (fraud, defects, disease).
why_it_matters: Needs special handling (re-weighting, re-sampling, the right metrics) or the model simply learns to predict the majority class.

definition: The standard Python library for classic ML.
why_it_matters: Where almost every tutorial's `.fit()` and `.predict()` come from.

definition: The basic unit: a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function.
why_it_matters: Everything in deep learning is millions of these wired together; each one is just multiply, add, squash.

definition: The numbers inside the model that training adjusts. "7B" means 7 billion of them.
why_it_matters: The parameters are the model. Download the weights and you have it; change them and you have a different model.

definition: The intermediate values flowing through the network for one input (as opposed to the weights, which are fixed during inference).
why_it_matters: Weights are what the model knows; activations are what it is thinking right now about this input. Interpretability studies activations.

definition: A group of neurons computed together. Layers between input and output are hidden layers.
why_it_matters: "Deep" simply means many hidden layers; each adds a level of abstraction.

definition: Stacked fully-connected layers. Also the second half of every Transformer block.
why_it_matters: The plainest neural network; inside an LLM the FFN layers are where most of the parameters, and most of the stored knowledge, live.

definition: Non-linearity applied after a layer. GELU and SiLU are the ones used inside LLMs.
why_it_matters: Without it, stacking layers would collapse into one straight line. The non-linearity is what lets networks learn curves and complex rules.

definition: Turns a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to 1.
why_it_matters: How the model expresses "70% sure the next word is 'Paris'". Applied at the output and inside attention.

definition: Raw, unnormalised scores that come out before softmax.
why_it_matters: What the model actually computes; softmax just converts them to probabilities. Temperature acts on logits.

definition: Representing a category as a vector of zeros with a single 1 at that category's position.
why_it_matters: The naive way to feed words to a network. Embeddings replace it with dense vectors that carry meaning.

definition: Running an input through the network to get an output.
why_it_matters: Inference is just a forward pass; training is a forward pass plus a backward pass.

definition: A number measuring how wrong the output is; training minimises it. Cross-entropy for classification and next-token prediction, mean squared error for regression.
why_it_matters: Defines what "better" means. The whole of training is "make this number smaller".

definition: The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to the loss, by applying the chain rule backwards through the network.
why_it_matters: Tells every one of the billions of weights which direction to move. Without it, training deep networks would be hopeless.

definition: The direction and size of change in loss for each weight.
why_it_matters: The "which way is downhill" signal; backprop computes it, the optimizer follows it.

definition: Nudge each weight a small step against its gradient. Stochastic gradient descent does this on one mini-batch per step.
why_it_matters: The learning rule behind all of deep learning: take a small step downhill, repeat millions of times.

definition: Smarter update rules that adapt the step size per weight using running averages of gradients. AdamW is the default for Transformers.
why_it_matters: Makes training converge faster and more reliably than plain gradient descent, at the cost of extra memory per weight.

definition: How big each update step is.
why_it_matters: The single most important hyperparameter. Too high and training blows up; too low and it never gets anywhere.

definition: The group of examples processed in one step before the weights are updated.
why_it_matters: Bigger batches use the GPU better and give smoother gradients; smaller ones fit in memory. A knob you will see in every training script.

definition: One full pass over the training set.
why_it_matters: Classic ML trains for many epochs; LLM pre-training usually sees each token about once.

definition: Forward pass → loss → backward pass → optimizer step, repeated. Everything from a toy MLP to a frontier LLM runs this loop.
why_it_matters: If you understand this loop (Map 3) you understand what "training" means at every stage of Map 2.

definition: How the weights are set before training starts: small random numbers with a carefully chosen scale.
why_it_matters: A bad starting scale makes gradients vanish or explode on step one; good initialization makes deep networks trainable.

definition: Randomly switch off neurons during training.
why_it_matters: Forces the network not to rely on any single neuron, which reduces overfitting.

definition: Shrink the weights slightly every step (L2-style regularization).
why_it_matters: Keeps weights small, which helps generalisation; the "W" in AdamW.

definition: Rescaling activations so they stay in a healthy range. LayerNorm and its cheaper cousin RMSNorm are the ones used in Transformers.
why_it_matters: Keeps training stable in very deep networks; without it, values drift and training diverges.

definition: Add a layer's input to its output. Forms the residual stream of a Transformer.
why_it_matters: Lets gradients flow straight through dozens of layers, which is what makes 100-layer networks trainable at all.

definition: Gradients shrinking to nothing or blowing up as they flow back through many layers.
why_it_matters: The historical reason deep networks did not work before ~2012; residuals, normalization and better initialization fixed it.

definition: A learned vector of numbers representing a token, word, image or item so that similar things end up close together.
why_it_matters: How a computer represents meaning: "king" and "queen" become nearby points. The input to every LLM and the basis of semantic search.

definition: The internal vector space in which the model represents meaning.
why_it_matters: Where the model "thinks": arithmetic on these vectors (king − man + woman ≈ queen) is what makes them useful.

definition: The assumptions an architecture builds in: CNNs assume nearby pixels matter, RNNs assume order, Transformers assume very little.
why_it_matters: Explains why CNNs need less data for images and why Transformers need huge data but scale further.

definition: A multi-dimensional array (vector, matrix, and beyond).
why_it_matters: The data type everything in deep learning is made of; a "shape" like [batch, tokens, 768] tells you what is flowing where.

definition: Framework machinery (PyTorch) that records every operation so backprop can be computed automatically.
why_it_matters: Why you never write backprop by hand: call `loss.backward()` and PyTorch does the calculus.

definition: A network using small sliding filters. The classic architecture for images (LeNet, AlexNet, ResNet).
why_it_matters: Detects the same pattern anywhere in an image with few parameters. Still the workhorse for vision on small devices.

definition: Networks that process sequences one step at a time with a memory state. They dominated language tasks before Transformers replaced them.
why_it_matters: Worked for sequences but could not be parallelised and forgot long-range context. Attention fixed both problems.

definition: An encoder reads an input sequence, a decoder writes an output sequence (early translation models).
why_it_matters: Attention was invented to fix seq2seq's bottleneck of squeezing a whole sentence into one vector.

definition: Networks trained to compress and then reconstruct their input. The variational version learns a smooth latent space you can sample from.
why_it_matters: Learns compact representations without labels; the VAE is also the compressor inside Stable Diffusion.

definition: A generator and a discriminator trained against each other.
why_it_matters: Produced the first photorealistic generated faces (2014–2020); mostly replaced by diffusion models, which are easier to train.

definition: Generates images (and audio, video) by learning to reverse a gradual noising process.
why_it_matters: The engine behind Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2/3 and Midjourney: start from noise, remove it step by step toward the prompt.

definition: The collection of text (web pages, books, code, transcripts) the model learns from. Trillions of tokens for frontier models.
why_it_matters: The model knows only what was in here. Quality and mix of the corpus decide much of the model's quality.

definition: The unit the model actually reads and writes. Usually a word piece; roughly ¾ of an English word on average.
why_it_matters: Everything is counted in tokens: context limits, speed, and your API bill.

definition: Converts text to token IDs and back. Built before pre-training and frozen with the model.
why_it_matters: Explains odd behaviour like miscounting letters in a word: the model never sees letters, only token IDs.

definition: Each token has an integer ID in the vocabulary. The model consumes and produces IDs; detokenization turns IDs back into text.
why_it_matters: The model is a function from integers to integers; text is only at the edges.

definition: The most common tokenizer algorithm: start from bytes or characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair. Used by GPT and Llama models.
why_it_matters: Lets the model handle any string (even emoji and typos) with a fixed vocabulary, while keeping common words as single tokens.

definition: Other tokenizer algorithms and libraries: BERT uses WordPiece, many open models use SentencePiece, OpenAI models use tiktoken.
why_it_matters: Different names in different tutorials, same job: text ↔ tokens.

definition: The set of all tokens the model knows, typically 32k to 200k entries.
why_it_matters: A bigger vocabulary means fewer tokens per sentence (cheaper, faster) but a bigger output layer.

definition: Tokenizers are trained mostly on English, so other languages split into more tokens per word. Polish text typically costs about 2× the tokens of the same text in English (1.5–2.5× depending on the tokenizer; newer 200k+ vocabularies do better, older 32k ones worse).
why_it_matters: The same prompt in Polish uses more of the context window and costs more than in English.

definition: Control tokens marking beginning / end of sequence, padding, or chat roles (user, assistant, tool).
why_it_matters: How the model knows where a message starts and ends, and when to stop generating.

definition: The maximum number of tokens the model can take in at once (prompt plus answer): 8k, 128k, 1M.
why_it_matters: The model's working memory. Anything outside it does not exist for the model; everything inside costs compute and money.

definition: An ordered list of tokens. Models are trained on fixed-length chunks of the corpus.
why_it_matters: "Sequence length" in a training script is how much text the model sees per example.

definition: Training data is cut into chunks; the target is the same chunk shifted by one token, so every position has a "next token" to predict. (Raschka chapter 2.)
why_it_matters: How free labels are created from raw text: the text itself is the answer key.

definition: Removing junk, duplicates and low-quality text before training.
why_it_matters: One of the biggest levers on model quality: cleaner data makes a smarter model at the same size.

definition: The proportions of web, code, books, maths, multilingual text in the training set.
why_it_matters: Decides what the model is good at: more code in the mix makes a better coder.

definition: Training text generated by another model.
why_it_matters: Fills gaps where real data is scarce (maths steps, rare languages) and is now a major ingredient of both pre- and post-training.

definition: People who write ideal answers, rank outputs or label data for SFT and reward models (companies like Scale AI and Surge AI).
why_it_matters: The human work behind "human feedback"; its quality shapes how the model behaves.

definition: Well-known public web-scale datasets used as pre-training corpora.
why_it_matters: When a video says a model was trained on "the internet", these are the concrete datasets it means.

definition: The exact text format (role markers, special tokens) used to serialise a conversation into tokens. Each model family has its own.
why_it_matters: A conversation is just one long token sequence with markers; getting the template wrong is a common cause of bad outputs with open models.

definition: The neural architecture from the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need": stacked blocks of attention plus feed-forward layers.
why_it_matters: Processes all tokens in parallel (fast on GPUs) and lets any token look at any other (long-range context). Both are why it won.

definition: A mechanism that lets each token look at other tokens and weigh how relevant they are, so context flows across the whole sequence in one step.
why_it_matters: How the model knows that "it" refers to "the cat" ten words earlier. The core idea of modern AI.

definition: Attention where tokens attend to other tokens of the same sequence.
why_it_matters: Lets every word be interpreted in the light of every other word in the text.

definition: Three projections of each token. A token's query is compared with every key to get weights, which are then applied to the values.
why_it_matters: Think of a lookup: the query asks a question, keys say what each token offers, values are what gets returned.

definition: The actual attention formula: softmax(QKᵀ / √d) · V.
why_it_matters: The one formula every video shows. Dividing by √d keeps the softmax from saturating so gradients stay healthy.

definition: Several attention operations run in parallel (heads), each free to focus on a different kind of relationship.
why_it_matters: One head can track grammar while another tracks topic. More heads, richer understanding.

definition: Variants that share key/value projections across heads. Llama 2 (70B), Llama 3, Mistral and most 2024+ models use GQA.
why_it_matters: Shrinks the KV cache several-fold, so inference is faster and cheaper with almost no quality loss.

definition: DeepSeek's alternative to GQA: keys and values are compressed into a small latent vector per token, which is what the KV cache stores; they are expanded again when attention runs (DeepSeek-V2, V3, R1).
why_it_matters: Cuts the KV cache far more than GQA with no quality loss, which is how DeepSeek serves long contexts cheaply.

definition: Masking so a token can only attend to earlier tokens.
why_it_matters: Stops the model from cheating by looking at the answer during training, and is what makes it generate left to right.

definition: The tensor that marks which positions may attend to which (causal mask, padding mask).
why_it_matters: The practical implementation of "no peeking ahead" and "ignore padding".

definition: Every token compares itself with every other, so compute and memory grow with the square of the sequence length.
why_it_matters: Why long context is expensive and why FlashAttention, sliding windows and state-space models exist.

definition: Limiting each token to attend only to the last N tokens (sliding window), optionally keeping a few initial tokens always visible (attention sinks).
why_it_matters: Makes very long inputs affordable at some cost in long-range recall; used in the original Mistral 7B and, mixed with global layers, in Gemma 2/3 and gpt-oss.

definition: The decoder attending to the encoder's outputs, in encoder-decoder models.
why_it_matters: How a translator model reads the source sentence while writing the target one.

definition: A Transformer with causal self-attention only, trained to predict the next token. The dominant LLM design.
why_it_matters: Simplest design that scales; one model does understanding and generation. Almost every chat model is this.

definition: A bidirectional Transformer good at understanding, classification and embeddings, but not at generating text.
why_it_matters: Still the usual choice for cheap classification and small, fast embedding models, because it reads both directions at once; many top-scoring embedding models are now built on decoder-only LLMs.

definition: An encoder reads the input, a decoder writes the output.
why_it_matters: Natural for translation and summarisation; largely displaced by decoder-only models that do everything.

definition: How the model knows token order, since attention by itself is order-blind. Sinusoidal in 2017, learned in GPT-2.
why_it_matters: Without it, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look identical to the model.

definition: Today's standard positional scheme: encodes position by rotating the Q and K vectors so attention depends on relative distance.
why_it_matters: Does not extrapolate well on its own, but can be cheaply stretched to longer contexts (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN), which is what makes 128k-token contexts practical.

definition: A positional scheme with no position embeddings at all: a penalty proportional to the query–key distance is subtracted from each attention score, with a different slope per head (used by MPT and BLOOM).
why_it_matters: Trains on short sequences and extrapolates to longer ones; the main rival to RoPE before RoPE won.

definition: The vector representing a token at a given layer; the residual stream's value at that point.
why_it_matters: What gets passed from block to block, and what the LM head reads at the end. "Hidden size" = its length.

definition: One unit of [attention → add & norm → feed-forward → add & norm]. Models stack 32 to 100+ of them.
why_it_matters: The repeating unit; a model is this block copied N times with different weights. See Map 5.

definition: The per-token two-layer network after attention; it holds most of the parameters. SwiGLU is the gated variant most modern models use.
why_it_matters: Attention moves information between tokens; the FFN processes it. Facts the model "knows" are mostly stored here.

definition: The running vector per token that every block adds its contribution to.
why_it_matters: Each block reads from and writes to it, so information from early layers survives to the end.

definition: A 2026 variant of the residual stream (Moonshot AI): instead of adding every earlier layer's output with a fixed weight of 1, each layer attends over earlier outputs with learned, softmax-normalised weights.
why_it_matters: Small but consistent gains for ~4% extra training cost; a sign that even the residual stream is still being redesigned.

definition: Whether normalization happens before or after each sub-layer. Pre-norm with RMSNorm is the modern choice.
why_it_matters: Pre-norm trains more stably at scale, which is why GPT-2 onward switched to it.

definition: Normalize the query and key vectors (RMSNorm or LayerNorm) before computing attention scores (Gemma 3, OLMo 2, Qwen3).
why_it_matters: Stops attention logits from blowing up, which removes a common cause of loss spikes and allows higher learning rates.

definition: The main shape hyperparameters of a Transformer: vector width per token, number of attention heads, number of stacked blocks.
why_it_matters: Three numbers that describe a model's shape; parameter count follows from them (Map 5).

definition: The final linear layer mapping each token's hidden state to logits over the vocabulary.
why_it_matters: Turns the model's internal vector into "a score for every possible next token".

definition: Reusing the token-embedding matrix as the LM head.
why_it_matters: Saves a large chunk of parameters in small models (a third of GPT-2's).

definition: Replaces each feed-forward layer with several experts and a router that activates only a few per token (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-MoE).
why_it_matters: Huge knowledge capacity with the compute cost of a much smaller model: a 235B model that runs like a 22B one.

definition: A dense model uses all parameters for every token; a sparse (MoE) model uses a subset.
why_it_matters: Explains names like "235B-A22B": 235B parameters total, 22B active per token.

definition: An exact but much faster, memory-efficient GPU implementation of attention.
why_it_matters: Same maths, 2–4× faster and far less memory, by being clever about GPU memory traffic. An engineering trick, not a new architecture.

definition: Alternative sequence layers whose cost grows linearly with sequence length. Often mixed with attention layers.
why_it_matters: A bet on cheaper long context; hybrids keep a few attention layers for precise recall.

definition: A Transformer applied to image patches as if they were tokens.
why_it_matters: Showed the same architecture works for images, which is what makes multimodal models possible.

definition: The first and most expensive phase: train the randomly-initialised model on a massive corpus by predicting the next token.
why_it_matters: Where the model learns language, facts and reasoning. Everything after only shapes how that knowledge is used.

definition: The pre-training objective: given the tokens so far, output a probability distribution over the next one.
why_it_matters: A deceptively simple task: predicting the next word well enough requires understanding grammar, facts and logic.

definition: During training the model sees the true previous tokens as input, not its own guesses, so all positions train in one parallel pass.
why_it_matters: Why training is fast (whole sequence at once) while generation is slow (one token at a time).

definition: The BERT-style objective: hide random tokens and predict them from both sides.
why_it_matters: Produces excellent understanding models (and embeddings) but not text generators.

definition: The raw pre-trained model: continues text well, does not yet follow instructions or chat.
why_it_matters: Ask it a question and it may continue with more questions. Post-training turns it into an assistant.

definition: A saved snapshot of the weights (and optimizer state) during or after training.
why_it_matters: Lets a run resume after a crash and lets researchers compare the model at different points.

definition: The standard measure of how well a language model predicts text: exp(loss). Lower is better.
why_it_matters: A perplexity of 10 means the model is, on average, as uncertain as choosing among 10 equally likely tokens.

definition: Training loss over steps, alongside loss on held-out data. Validation loss rising while training loss falls means overfitting.
why_it_matters: The main thing engineers watch during a run; a smooth downward curve means learning is working.

definition: Sudden jumps in the loss during a long run: a bad batch, too high a learning rate or numerical trouble.
why_it_matters: The nightmare of large training runs; gradient clipping, lower learning rates and restarting from a checkpoint are the usual fixes.

definition: Ramp the learning rate up at the start, hold, then decay it toward the end.
why_it_matters: Warmup prevents early blow-ups; decay lets the model settle into a good minimum. Standard practice for every LLM run.

definition: Cap the gradient norm so one bad batch cannot blow up training.
why_it_matters: A safety valve against exploding gradients and loss spikes.

definition: Sum gradients over several mini-batches before updating.
why_it_matters: Simulates a big batch on a small GPU, so you can train with less memory.

definition: Ordering training data from easy to hard, or changing the data mix over the course of training.
why_it_matters: Can make training faster and the final model better than feeding everything in random order.

definition: Using lower-precision numbers for speed and memory while keeping a master copy of the weights in FP32. BF16 is the norm; FP8 is arriving.
why_it_matters: Roughly doubles throughput and halves activation memory versus FP32, with no loss in quality when done right; weight and optimizer memory stay similar because the FP32 master copy remains.

definition: The total floating-point operations a training run uses, roughly 6 × parameters × tokens.
why_it_matters: Compute is the currency labs plan in; "10²⁵ FLOPs" is how regulators and papers describe a model's size of effort.

definition: What fraction of the GPUs' theoretical peak compute the training run actually achieves (typically 30–50%).
why_it_matters: The efficiency score of a training run; low MFU means expensive GPUs sitting idle waiting for data or communication.

definition: The empirical finding that loss improves smoothly and predictably as you scale parameters, data and compute together.
why_it_matters: Why labs bet billions: you can predict how much better a 10× bigger model will be before training it.

definition: The 2022 rule of thumb of about 20 training tokens per parameter for a given training budget. Modern models are deliberately over-trained far beyond it.
why_it_matters: Why an 8B model trained on 15T tokens beats older 70B models: small models are cheaper to serve, so extra training pays off.

definition: Capabilities that appear only once models pass a certain scale (a contested idea).
why_it_matters: The argument for scaling: arithmetic or multi-step reasoning seemed to switch on at size.

definition: Three ways to split training across GPUs: by data batches, by slicing layers across devices, or by giving different layers to different devices.
why_it_matters: How a model too big for one GPU is trained on thousands at once.

definition: Techniques that shard the weights, gradients and optimizer state across GPUs.
why_it_matters: Lets models far bigger than one GPU's memory train without complex manual splitting.

definition: Keep pre-training a base model on new domain data (medical, legal, a new language, your company's docs) before any instruction tuning.
why_it_matters: The way to add deep domain knowledge or a new language; much cheaper than training from scratch, much heavier than fine-tuning.

definition: The final pre-training phase on a higher-quality data mix with a decaying learning rate.
why_it_matters: Increasingly where labs tune knowledge quality and inject maths, code and long-context ability.

definition: Everything the lab does after pre-training to make the model useful and safe: SFT, preference optimization, reinforcement learning.
why_it_matters: Turns a text-completer into an assistant. Most of what you feel as the model's "personality" was shaped here.

definition: Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller, targeted dataset. Labs do it (post-training) and you can do it (section 9).
why_it_matters: Same mechanics as pre-training, far less data. The word means two different stages depending on who is speaking.

definition: Train on curated prompt → ideal-answer pairs so the model learns to follow instructions and hold a conversation.
why_it_matters: Teaches the model the format of being helpful: answer the question, use the chat template, stop when done.

definition: The model after post-training. What you actually talk to.
why_it_matters: The "-Instruct" or "-Chat" suffix on a model name means it has been through this stage.

definition: Making the model's behaviour match human intentions and values; often summarised as helpful, harmless and honest (HHH).
why_it_matters: Both a goal (the model behaves as intended) and the name of the RLHF / safety part of post-training.

definition: Humans rank model outputs → train a reward model on those rankings → use RL (PPO) to push the model toward higher-reward answers.
why_it_matters: Makes answers more helpful and polite than SFT alone, because it optimises for what people actually prefer. The technique behind ChatGPT.

definition: A model trained to score how good an answer is, standing in for human judgement during reinforcement learning.
why_it_matters: Lets RL run millions of times without a human in the loop: the reward model is the automated judge.

definition: "Answer A is better than answer B" data used to train reward models or directly in DPO.
why_it_matters: Cheaper to collect than ideal answers: comparing two outputs is easier than writing a perfect one.

definition: The RL algorithm classically used in RLHF. Updates the policy in small clipped steps.
why_it_matters: Keeps RL training stable: small steps mean the model cannot suddenly wander into nonsense.

definition: Trains directly on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss, skipping the reward model and the RL loop.
why_it_matters: Gets most of RLHF's benefit with a fraction of the complexity, which is why open-model teams love it.

definition: A PPO variant that samples a group of answers to the same prompt and scores each relative to the group, with no separate value model. Used by DeepSeek-R1.
why_it_matters: Cheaper and simpler than PPO, and it turned out to be the recipe for training reasoning models.

definition: The Qwen team's 2025 successor to GRPO: the importance ratio and clipping are computed per whole sequence instead of per token. Used to train the Qwen3 Instruct, Coder and Thinking models.
why_it_matters: More stable RL training, especially for Mixture-of-Experts models, where token-level GRPO tends to collapse.

definition: On-policy methods (PPO, GRPO) learn from answers the current model just generated; off-policy methods (DPO on a fixed dataset) learn from stored data.
why_it_matters: On-policy is more expensive but keeps improving the model on its own mistakes; off-policy is cheap but can go stale.

definition: Use an AI, guided by a written set of principles (a constitution), to produce the feedback instead of, or alongside, humans. Anthropic's approach.
why_it_matters: Scales feedback far beyond what human raters can produce, and makes the rules explicit and inspectable.

definition: Reinforcement learning where the reward is an automatic check: did the maths answer match, did the unit tests pass.
why_it_matters: No reward model to fool: when the answer is checkable, RL can push the model far beyond human demonstrations. The key ingredient of reasoning models.

definition: An ORM scores only the final answer; a PRM scores each step of the reasoning.
why_it_matters: Step-level rewards give the model more precise feedback on where it went wrong, at a higher labelling cost.

definition: A model post-trained to produce a long chain of thought before answering (OpenAI o-series, DeepSeek-R1, Claude extended thinking, Gemini thinking).
why_it_matters: Much more accurate on maths, code and multi-step problems, in exchange for more tokens and latency.

definition: The number of tokens a reasoning model may spend thinking before it answers; often a setting you control. Reasoning tokens are usually billed as output.
why_it_matters: Lets you trade cost and speed for accuracy per request.

definition: Spending more compute at answer time (longer thinking, multiple samples, search) to get better answers, instead of only training a bigger model.
why_it_matters: The second scaling axis: the same model gets smarter if you let it think longer.

definition: Reinforcement learning on whole tasks that involve many steps and tool calls, not single answers.
why_it_matters: How models are trained to be good at long coding sessions and browsing, not only at one-shot replies.

definition: A term in the RL objective keeping the trained model close to the SFT model.
why_it_matters: Stops the model from drifting into gibberish that happens to score well with the reward model.

definition: The model finding ways to get high reward without actually being good: verbosity, confident tone, telling the grader what it wants.
why_it_matters: Why RL needs careful rewards: optimise a flawed score and you get a flawed model.

definition: The tendency to agree with the user over telling the truth.
why_it_matters: A known side effect of optimising for human approval; worth remembering when a model agrees with you too easily.

definition: Generate N answers, keep the best according to a judge or reward model, then train on those.
why_it_matters: A simple, strong post-training method: let the model teach itself from its own best attempts.

definition: Train a smaller student model to imitate a bigger teacher's outputs.
why_it_matters: How small, cheap models get surprisingly capable: they copy the behaviour of a frontier model.

definition: Averaging or combining the weights of several fine-tuned models into one.
why_it_matters: Combines skills from different fine-tunes without retraining; cheap and oddly effective.

definition: Post-training the model to decline harmful requests and handle sensitive topics carefully.
why_it_matters: Why a model says no to some requests; the behaviour is learned here, not hard-coded.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Taking an open-weight model (or an API fine-tuning endpoint) and training it further on your own examples to change its style, format or domain behaviour.
why_it_matters: Makes a general model behave your way: consistent format, your tone, your domain's conventions, often with a smaller and cheaper model.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Update all the weights.
why_it_matters: Highest quality ceiling but needs the most GPU memory and risks forgetting general skills.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: A family of methods that freeze the model and train only a small set of extra parameters.
why_it_matters: Fine-tune a big model on a single GPU and store the result as a tiny file.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: The most popular PEFT method: learn small low-rank matrices that are added to the attention and feed-forward weights.
why_it_matters: Trains ~1% of the parameters for most of the benefit; the adapter is a small file (tens to a couple of hundred MB) you can swap in and out.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantized base model.
why_it_matters: Lets you fine-tune a 65–70B model on a single 48 GB GPU, or a 7–13B model on a consumer card.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Other PEFT flavours: small bottleneck layers inserted in the network, or learned soft-prompt vectors prepended to the input.
why_it_matters: Same goal as LoRA (cheap adaptation), different mechanics; LoRA won on simplicity.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: LoRA hyperparameters controlling adapter size and how strongly it is scaled.
why_it_matters: Higher rank = more capacity and memory; typical values are 8–64.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Adding the trained LoRA matrices into the base weights to produce a single standalone model.
why_it_matters: Removes the small inference overhead of a separate adapter and gives you one file to deploy.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: A small new output layer placed on top of the model for a specific task (e.g. spam / not spam), replacing the LM head. (Raschka chapter 6.)
why_it_matters: The simplest fine-tune: reuse everything the model knows, train only the last layer for your labels.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Fine-tuning on a narrow dataset erodes the general abilities the model had before.
why_it_matters: Why you keep the learning rate low, mix in general data, and prefer LoRA: to add a skill without losing the others.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Specialising a general model to a field: legal, medical, your codebase, your product's tone.
why_it_matters: Makes the model fluent in your world's vocabulary and conventions.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: The prompt → completion pairs you fine-tune on. Quality matters more than quantity; hundreds to a few thousand good examples often suffice.
why_it_matters: Your main lever: the model will copy whatever these examples do, including their mistakes.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Standard JSON layouts for instruction data: Alpaca (instruction / input / output), ShareGPT (conversations), or OpenAI-style messages lists.
why_it_matters: The format most fine-tuning tools expect; converting your data into one of these is step one.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Open weights means you can download and fine-tune the parameters (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma). True open source also releases the data and training code (OLMo).
why_it_matters: Open weights are what let you fine-tune and self-host; "open source" is usually a looser claim.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: Fine-tuning a closed model through the provider's API: you upload examples, they train and host the result.
why_it_matters: Fine-tuning without GPUs or ops; the trade-off is lock-in and less control.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
term: Hugging Face PEFT / TRL / Unsloth / Axolotl
definition: The standard libraries and tools for running LoRA, SFT and DPO on open models.
why_it_matters: The tools most fine-tuning tutorials use; Unsloth is the fast, memory-light one for single GPUs.

section_title: Adapting a model to your task
definition: A held-out slice of your own examples used to check the fine-tune actually improved things.
why_it_matters: The only way to know your fine-tune helped and did not just overfit your examples.

definition: Using a trained model to produce output. No weights change.
why_it_matters: What every API call and chat message is. The cost and speed of AI products are decided here.

definition: Produce one token, append it to the input, run again, until a stop token or the max length is reached.
why_it_matters: Why text appears word by word, and why long answers take proportionally longer.

definition: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass (compute-bound). Decode produces tokens one at a time (memory-bound).
why_it_matters: Explains the two numbers you feel: a pause before the first token (prefill), then a steady stream (decode).

definition: Storing the keys and values of all previous tokens so each new token does not recompute them.
why_it_matters: Makes generation many times faster; its memory size is the main limit on long contexts and many parallel users.

definition: How the next token is chosen from the probability distribution the model outputs.
why_it_matters: The same model can sound careful or creative depending only on this choice.

definition: Always pick the most probable token.
why_it_matters: Deterministic and fast, but tends to repeat itself and miss better overall sentences.

definition: Pick the next token randomly according to the model's probabilities.
why_it_matters: Gives variety and more natural text; the reason the same prompt gives different answers.

definition: Scales the logits before softmax. Low values make output focused and near-deterministic, high values make it diverse and random. 0 is effectively greedy.
why_it_matters: Your main creativity knob: low for code and facts, higher for brainstorming.

definition: Only sample from the k most likely tokens, or from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.
why_it_matters: Cuts off the long tail of nonsense tokens so sampling stays creative but coherent.

definition: Keep several candidate sequences and expand the best ones.
why_it_matters: Finds higher-probability whole sentences; common in translation, rarely used in chat because it sounds bland.

definition: Lower the probability of tokens that have already appeared.
why_it_matters: Stops the model from looping on the same phrase.

definition: Restricting sampling so the output must follow a grammar or JSON schema.
why_it_matters: Guarantees valid JSON or a fixed set of choices, rather than hoping the model complies.

definition: The log-probabilities of generated tokens, which APIs can expose.
why_it_matters: A cheap confidence signal: low probability on a key token is a hint the model is guessing.

definition: The limit on output length, and strings that end generation early.
why_it_matters: Controls cost and prevents run-on answers.

definition: Sending tokens to the client as they are generated.
why_it_matters: Makes a 10-second answer feel instant because the user starts reading immediately.

definition: Time to first token measures prefill. Time per output token (the gap between tokens, also called inter-token latency) measures decode; tokens per second is its inverse.
why_it_matters: The numbers users feel: optimise TTFT for chat, TPOT for long outputs.

definition: Serving many requests at once by batching their decode steps. Continuous batching slots new requests in mid-stream.
why_it_matters: Serves many more users per GPU, which is what makes API prices possible.

definition: Managing the KV cache like virtual-memory pages so GPU memory is not wasted. vLLM is the open-source engine that popularised it.
why_it_matters: Fits more simultaneous requests in the same GPU memory, roughly 2–4× the throughput.

definition: Storing weights (and sometimes activations) in fewer bits.
why_it_matters: Cuts memory 2–4× and speeds up inference, at a small quality cost; how a 70B model fits on one GPU or a laptop.

definition: Common quantized formats and methods. GGUF is the format llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio use.
why_it_matters: When a download page lists "Q4_K_M", it is a 4-bit GGUF file ready for local use.

definition: A small draft model proposes several tokens, the big model verifies them in one pass.
why_it_matters: Same output as the big model, noticeably faster, because verifying is cheaper than generating.

definition: Software that loads weights and serves requests efficiently: the first four for servers, the last two for laptops.
why_it_matters: The difference between a demo and a production service; they handle batching, caching and memory for you.

definition: Reusing the KV cache for a repeated prefix (a long system prompt, a set of documents) across requests.
why_it_matters: Cuts cost and latency sharply when many requests share the same long beginning.

definition: Caching whole answers keyed by the meaning of the question, so a similar question returns the stored answer without calling the model.
why_it_matters: Avoids paying for the same answer twice when users ask the same thing in different words.

definition: Sending each request to the cheapest model likely to handle it, escalating to a bigger one only when needed.
why_it_matters: Big cost savings with little quality loss, because most requests are easy.

definition: Providers offer discounted non-urgent batch processing, and cap how many requests and tokens you can send per minute.
why_it_matters: Shapes system design: batch what can wait, queue and retry for the rest.

definition: Running models beyond their trained length with positional scaling tricks (RoPE scaling, YaRN) and better attention kernels.
why_it_matters: How 4k-context models became 128k; recall at the far end of the window is still weaker.

definition: Running small quantized models on phones and laptops with no server.
why_it_matters: Private, offline and free per use; the trade-off is a much smaller model.

definition: Rule of thumb: parameters × bytes per weight. A 7B model is about 14 GB in 16-bit and about 4 GB at 4-bit, plus the KV cache.
why_it_matters: Quick way to know whether a model fits your GPU or laptop before downloading it.

definition: The text you send to the model: instructions, context, question.
why_it_matters: The model's entire view of your task; everything it does not say, the model does not know.

definition: Instructions set by the developer that frame the whole conversation: persona, rules, available tools, output format.
why_it_matters: Your main control surface as an engineer; most product behaviour is written here, not trained.

definition: Crafting prompts to get reliable results: clear instructions, examples, explicit output format, role, constraints. Prompts are versioned and tested like code.
why_it_matters: The cheapest and fastest way to improve a model's output; always the first thing to try.

definition: Asking with no examples versus including a few worked examples in the prompt.
why_it_matters: A couple of examples in the prompt often beat pages of instructions.

definition: The model's ability to pick up a task from examples in the prompt without any weight updates.
why_it_matters: Why few-shot works: the model adapts on the fly, no training needed.

definition: Asking the model to reason step by step before answering.
why_it_matters: Noticeably more accurate on reasoning tasks because the model gets to "use scratch paper"; reasoning models bake this in.

definition: Sample several answers and take the most common one.
why_it_matters: A simple way to buy accuracy with more compute; a form of test-time scaling you can do from the outside.

definition: Explore several reasoning paths, evaluate them, and expand the promising ones, instead of one linear chain.
why_it_matters: Better on hard planning problems; the application-level cousin of MCTS.

definition: Forcing the model to answer in a machine-readable format, often validated against a schema.
why_it_matters: Makes model output safe to parse in code, which any real integration needs.

definition: The model emits a structured request (call get_weather with city = Kraków), your code runs it and returns the result for the model to continue.
why_it_matters: Lets the model act on the world and fetch live data instead of guessing from memory.

definition: An LLM in a loop: observe → decide → act with tools → observe the result, until the task is done.
why_it_matters: Turns a chatbot into something that completes multi-step tasks: fixing a bug, booking a trip, researching a question.

definition: A workflow is a fixed sequence of LLM calls you program; an agent decides its own next step at runtime.
why_it_matters: Workflows are predictable and cheap; agents are flexible and harder to control. Use the simplest one that works.

definition: Patterns for structuring agents: interleaving reasoning and actions (ReAct), explicit plans, decomposition into sub-tasks, reflection.
why_it_matters: Known recipes that make agents more reliable than a bare loop.

definition: Several specialised agents (planner, coder, reviewer, researcher) coordinating on one task.
why_it_matters: Splits a big job into roles with separate contexts; helps on long tasks, adds coordination overhead.

definition: An open standard for connecting models to tools and data sources through a common server interface, so any MCP client can use any MCP server.
why_it_matters: Write a tool once, use it from every assistant: the "USB-C of AI tools". Your Spring AI servers speak this.

definition: A standard for agents from different vendors to discover each other and exchange tasks.
why_it_matters: MCP connects an agent to tools; A2A connects agents to agents.

definition: Agents that operate a screen, browser or terminal through screenshots, clicks and keystrokes.
why_it_matters: Lets a model use software that has no API, which is most software.

definition: Coding assistants that read a repository, edit files, run tests and iterate on their own. "Vibe coding" is building by describing what you want and accepting the result.
why_it_matters: The most widely adopted agent use case; changes how software gets written.

definition: Running an agent's code and tool calls in an isolated environment with limited permissions.
why_it_matters: Contains the damage when an agent makes a mistake or is tricked by prompt injection.

definition: Requiring a person to approve certain steps (sending the email, deleting the file, paying).
why_it_matters: The standard safety net for agents taking real actions.

definition: Fetch relevant documents (search or vector database) and put them in the prompt so the model answers from your data.
why_it_matters: Gives the model knowledge it was never trained on, kept up to date, with sources, without any training.

definition: Vectors representing the meaning of a text chunk; similar texts land near each other. Produced by a separate embedding model.
why_it_matters: The basis of semantic search: find documents by meaning, not by matching keywords.

also_known_as: Qdrant; FAISS is the underlying index library
definition: A store that indexes embeddings for fast nearest-neighbour search.
why_it_matters: Finds the 10 most relevant chunks out of millions in milliseconds.

definition: Splitting documents into pieces small enough to embed and retrieve.
why_it_matters: Chunk size and overlap decide whether retrieval finds the right passage; one of the most-tuned RAG knobs.

definition: Searching by embedding similarity; hybrid search combines it with classic keyword search (BM25).
why_it_matters: Hybrid catches both "same meaning, different words" and exact identifiers like error codes.

definition: A second model that re-orders retrieved chunks by relevance before they go into the prompt.
why_it_matters: Cheap accuracy boost for RAG: retrieve 50 loosely, keep the best 5 precisely.

definition: Tying answers to retrieved sources so claims can be checked.
why_it_matters: Reduces hallucination and lets users verify; does not eliminate it.

definition: Managing everything in the context window (system prompt, retrieved docs, tool results, memory) so the model has what it needs and nothing more.
why_it_matters: Too little context and the model guesses; too much and it gets lost and costs more. Good agents are mostly good context management.

definition: Conversation history inside the context window versus facts stored outside and retrieved later.
why_it_matters: How an assistant remembers you across sessions: it is retrieval, not training.

definition: Input and output checks (classifiers, rules, schemas) placed around the model.
why_it_matters: Catches bad inputs and bad outputs the model itself might let through.

definition: An attack where untrusted content (a web page, an email, a document) contains instructions the model wrongly follows.
why_it_matters: The top security risk for agents: anything the model reads can try to give it orders.

definition: Using a strong model to grade another model's outputs at scale.
why_it_matters: Makes evaluation cheap enough to run on every change, like unit tests for prompts.

definition: Libraries wiring prompts, tools, retrieval and agents together.
why_it_matters: Save boilerplate; the concepts underneath are the ones in this section.

definition: Logging prompts, tool calls, tokens, cost and latency per request.
why_it_matters: You cannot improve an LLM app you cannot see; tracing shows why a given answer went wrong.

definition: Confident, fluent, wrong output.
why_it_matters: The model is predicting plausible text, not checking facts. RAG, tools and grounding reduce it; nothing eliminates it.

definition: APIs bill per input token and per output token. Output tokens cost more; cached input tokens cost less.
why_it_matters: Why prompt length, answer length and caching are the three cost levers.

definition: Any systematic measurement of model quality: benchmarks, human ratings, your own test sets.
why_it_matters: The only way to know whether a change helped; "it feels better" is not evidence.

definition: A fixed dataset plus a scoring rule for comparing models.
why_it_matters: How leaderboards are made; useful, and easy to game.

definition: Multiple-choice knowledge questions across 57 subjects; MMLU-Pro is the harder successor with 10 answer options across 14 disciplines.
why_it_matters: The classic general-knowledge score; now saturated for top models.

definition: Maths benchmarks from grade-school word problems up to competition level.
why_it_matters: Where reasoning models show the biggest jumps.

definition: Code benchmarks: generating functions from docstrings, and fixing real GitHub issues end to end.
why_it_matters: SWE-bench (Verified) is the number to watch for coding agents.

definition: Graduate-level science questions designed to be Google-proof.
why_it_matters: Tests deep expertise rather than memorised trivia.

definition: Benchmarks designed to stay hard: abstract visual puzzles (ARC-AGI) and expert questions across every field (HLE).
why_it_matters: The current frontier benchmarks; when older ones saturate, these are what headlines quote.

definition: Benchmarks scoring a model on multi-step tasks with tools, not single answers.
why_it_matters: Measure what matters for agents: finishing the job, not answering a question.

definition: Hide one fact in a very long document and check whether the model can retrieve it.
why_it_matters: The standard test of whether a long context window really works.

definition: The chance that at least one of k generated attempts is correct.
why_it_matters: Used for code and maths; pass@1 is what a user experiences, pass@10 shows the model's potential with search.

definition: Crowd-sourced blind comparisons of models, producing an Elo-style leaderboard.
why_it_matters: The closest thing to "which model do people prefer".

definition: Benchmark questions leaking into training data, inflating scores.
why_it_matters: Why benchmark numbers are treated with suspicion and why private test sets exist.

definition: The fraction of generated claims that are unsupported or false.
why_it_matters: The metric that matters most for RAG and research assistants.

definition: Systematic differences in model behaviour across groups of people.
why_it_matters: A legal and ethical requirement in hiring, lending and medicine.

definition: Stability of answers under rephrasing, typos, noise and adversarial inputs.
why_it_matters: A model that changes its answer over a comma is not production-ready.

definition: Methods that attribute a classic-ML prediction to the features that drove it.
why_it_matters: Required in regulated decisions; the classic-ML cousin of LLM interpretability.

definition: Deliberately attacking a model to find harmful or broken behaviour before release.
why_it_matters: Finds failures before users (or attackers) do.

definition: A prompt that tricks the model into ignoring its safety training.
why_it_matters: Safety behaviour is learned, not enforced, so defences are layered.

definition: A model declining harmless requests because they superficially resemble harmful ones.
why_it_matters: The other side of safety training; labs tune to minimise both harm and over-refusal.

definition: The field concerned with preventing harm from AI systems, from today's misuse to risks at larger scale. Responsible-scaling policies tie capability thresholds to the safeguards required before release.
why_it_matters: Where alignment, red teaming and safety levels come from; how labs commit to not shipping a model until matching safeguards exist.

definition: A model behaving differently when it suspects it is being tested, even hiding capabilities.
why_it_matters: A newer safety concern: evals are only trustworthy if the model cannot tell it is being evaluated.

definition: Techniques for humans to supervise models on tasks they cannot fully judge themselves (debate, AI-assisted review).
why_it_matters: The long-term question of alignment: how to check work better than yours.

definition: Studying what happens inside the network: which neurons, features and circuits do what.
why_it_matters: Lets researchers see why a model answered as it did, instead of a black box.

definition: Features are the interpretable concepts a model represents; superposition is the finding that it packs more features than it has neurons; Sparse Autoencoders are the tool that unmixes activations into those features.
why_it_matters: Found concrete concepts inside models (a "Golden Gate Bridge" feature); a path to steering and auditing.

definition: Documentation of a model's training, capabilities, limits and safety testing.
why_it_matters: Where to look before trusting a model.

definition: The massively parallel processor that does nearly all training and inference.
why_it_matters: Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplication, and GPUs do thousands of those in parallel; the reason AI progress tracks GPU supply.

definition: Google's custom accelerator, used for Gemini and available on Google Cloud.
why_it_matters: The main non-NVIDIA option at frontier scale.

definition: Accelerators designed specifically for running (or training) models, often with very high token speed.
why_it_matters: Why some providers serve 500+ tokens per second. (NVIDIA licensed Groq's technology in late 2025.)

definition: NVIDIA's GPU programming platform.
why_it_matters: The software moat: most frameworks and kernels target CUDA first, which keeps the ecosystem NVIDIA-first.

definition: The GPU's memory. 80 GB on an H100, 24 GB on a consumer RTX 4090.
why_it_matters: The hard limit on which models fit; most "can I run this?" questions are about VRAM.

definition: The error when a model, batch or KV cache does not fit in GPU memory.
why_it_matters: The most common error in any training or serving tutorial; fixes are smaller batch, quantization, gradient accumulation or a bigger GPU.

definition: High-speed interconnects joining thousands of GPUs into one training machine.
why_it_matters: Training a frontier model is as much a networking problem as a maths problem.

definition: The dominant deep-learning framework, and what Raschka's book uses. JAX (Google) and TensorFlow are the alternatives.
why_it_matters: Nearly every tutorial, paper and model release is in PyTorch; learn it first.

definition: The de-facto library and repository for open models, datasets and tokenizers.
why_it_matters: The GitHub of models: where you download weights and the library that loads them in three lines.

definition: The standard file format for storing model parameters safely (no arbitrary code on load).
why_it_matters: The file you actually download; safe to open unlike the older pickle format.

definition: Model size in billions of weights.
why_it_matters: A quick proxy for capability, memory and cost; the first number anyone quotes about a model.

definition: Hosted access to a model: you send tokens, you get tokens, you pay per token.
why_it_matters: The way most products use frontier models: no GPUs, no ops, pay per use.

definition: Companies that host open-weight models behind an API, often cheaper or faster than running them yourself. OpenRouter is an aggregator: one API that routes to many providers, closed and open.
why_it_matters: The middle path between a frontier API and self-hosting.

definition: A low-level program that runs on the GPU. FlashAttention is a kernel; Triton lets you write them in Python.
why_it_matters: Where the big speed-ups come from; most engineers never write one, but the names come up.

definition: Running inference engines as containers on GPU nodes, with autoscaling and the usual K8s plumbing.
why_it_matters: How a self-hosted model becomes a production service; the same platform skills you already have apply.

definition: Tools for running open-weight models on your own laptop or server.
why_it_matters: The fastest way to try an open model: one command, no cloud, full privacy.

definition: Macs share memory between CPU and GPU, so a Mac with 64–512 GB of unified memory can run models that need several consumer GPUs; MLX is Apple's framework for it.
why_it_matters: Why Mac laptops are popular for local LLMs despite having no NVIDIA GPU.

definition: Tools that log every training run's settings, loss curves and results.
why_it_matters: How teams compare hundreds of runs without losing track of what worked.

definition: Interactive Python environments; Colab and Kaggle give free GPU time.
why_it_matters: Where most tutorials (and Raschka's code) run; the cheapest way to get a GPU for an hour.

definition: A pair of encoders (image and text) trained so matching image–caption pairs get similar embeddings.
why_it_matters: Lets you search images with words and is the glue inside most image generators and vision-language models.

definition: An LLM with a vision encoder attached, so it can take images as input (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, Qwen-VL, LLaVA).
why_it_matters: Why you can paste a screenshot or a chart into a chat and ask about it.

definition: Images are cut into patches, encoded (usually by a ViT) and projected into the LLM's token space; a typical image becomes a few hundred to a few thousand tokens.
why_it_matters: Images are billed and context-limited as tokens, just like text.

definition: Diffusion run in the compressed latent space of a VAE instead of on raw pixels.
why_it_matters: Makes image generation many times cheaper, which is what put it on consumer GPUs.

definition: The denoising network inside a diffusion model: a U-Net in older models, a Transformer (DiT) in newer ones (Stable Diffusion 3, Flux, Sora).
why_it_matters: Another case of "Transformers ate the architecture"; same scaling story as LLMs.

definition: The text model that turns the prompt into conditioning vectors, and the knob (classifier-free guidance) controlling how strictly the image follows the prompt.
why_it_matters: Guidance scale is the image-generation equivalent of temperature: higher is more literal, lower is more creative.

definition: Add-ons that steer image generation with a sketch, pose, depth map or edge map in addition to text.
why_it_matters: Gives precise control over composition instead of hoping the prompt lands.

definition: LoRA adapters trained on a few dozen images to teach a diffusion model a style, product or face.
why_it_matters: The same LoRA idea from section 9, applied to images; the basis of the custom-model marketplaces.

definition: Regenerating part of an image, extending beyond its borders, or transforming an existing image guided by a prompt.
why_it_matters: The editing operations behind "generative fill" features.

definition: Speech to text. Whisper is the widely used open model.
why_it_matters: The first step of every voice assistant and the way meeting transcripts are made.

definition: Generating natural speech from text; cloning reproduces a specific voice from a short sample.
why_it_matters: The output side of voice assistants, audiobooks and dubbing; cloning is also why voice-based fraud is rising.

definition: Models that take audio in and produce audio out directly, with low latency, instead of chaining ASR → LLM → TTS.
why_it_matters: Makes natural, interruptible voice conversation possible.

definition: Single models trained on text, images, audio and video as input, producing text and speech (and sometimes images) as output.
why_it_matters: Where the frontier is heading: one model for every modality instead of a pipeline of specialists.

definition: Diffusion or transformer models that generate video clips from a prompt or an image.
why_it_matters: Same ideas as image generation, far more compute; the current showcase of generative AI, and a crowded market.

definition: Models that learn to predict how an environment evolves (the next frame, the result of an action), used in robotics and games.
why_it_matters: The argument that video generation is a step toward models that understand physics and planning.

definition: Extracting text and structure from scanned documents and PDFs; increasingly done by VLMs directly.
why_it_matters: How invoices, forms and old archives get into RAG pipelines.

definition: Embedding models that map images, text and audio into one shared vector space.
why_it_matters: Search a photo library with a sentence, or a product catalogue with a picture.

definition: Generated images, voices and videos impersonating real people, and the tools that try to detect or watermark them.
why_it_matters: The main misuse of generative media; provenance standards (C2PA) and watermarks are the response.
